title: Tiny Cameras Reveal the Secret Ocean Lives of Red-Footed Boobies
summary:
Red-footed boobies are large seabirds — about the size of a goose — with bright red webbed feet and blue and pink beaks. They nest on tropical islands but spend most of their time far out over the open ocean. Until recently, scientists knew very little about what they do out there.

In January 2024, four scientists splashed into the Indian Ocean near Nelsons Island, part of the Chagos Archipelago. They timed their arrival for midday, when sharks are less active. A ship dropped them as close as it could without hitting shallow coral reefs. From there, they jumped in and swam, towing waterproof bags full of camping gear, science equipment, food, and water — everything they'd need for two weeks.

"There's no feeling quite like being dropped off on an island by boat," said Alice Trevail, an ecologist at the University of Exeter.

Once on land, thousands of seabirds greeted them. The scientists had come to learn how red-footed boobies affect the plants and animals around them — and what they need to survive.

To track the birds, the team outfitted them with small, lightweight loggers and cameras. GPS units record location from satellite signals. Accelerometers log when a bird dives, swerves, or flaps its wings. Immersion loggers record when a bird hits the water. And in 2024, for the first time, the scientists added tiny video cameras to the birds' backs.

"Watching those videos is incredible," said Ruth Dunn, an ecologist at Lancaster University. She can now see when boobies fly alone, when they meet other birds, and how they catch fish.

The scientists work quickly — Trevail can tag a bird in about 10 minutes — to minimize disruption. They wear gloves and glasses because the birds have sharp beaks.

As tracking technology shrinks, scientists can study more species. And because researchers share data, they're building a clearer picture of birds that cross oceans and continents.
why_it_matters: Seabirds link the open ocean to island ecosystems, and knowing exactly where they feed is essential for deciding which parts of the sea to protect — especially as shrinking sensors let scientists track species that were once impossible to follow.

background_read: The Chagos Archipelago is a real group of roughly 60 small coral islands in the middle of the Indian Ocean, administered by Britain as the British Indian Ocean Territory. The largest island, Diego Garcia, hosts a US military base, and the surrounding waters became a marine protected area — one of the biggest in the world.
Because those reefs sit far from most human activity, they are among the least damaged in the Indian Ocean, which makes the area valuable for studying how seabirds and reefs affect each other.

Red-footed boobies are true ocean birds. They can travel hundreds of kilometres on a single fishing trip and come back to land mainly to breed, which is why so little was known about their lives at sea until tracking devices got small enough to carry.

The equipment the team used belongs to a field called biologging — fitting wild animals with small sensors. An accelerometer works on the same principle as the one in a smartphone or fitness tracker that counts your steps.
Alice Trevail is an ecologist at the University of Exeter and Ruth Dunn at Lancaster University, both research universities in England.

perspectives.description: For the first time the scientists can watch a booby's trip from the bird's own point of view: flying alone, meeting other birds, catching fish. That level of detail helps explain how these birds share the ocean and what habitats they depend on.

Catching and tagging wild birds is still a disruption, even when it takes only ten minutes. Added cameras and tags mean extra weight and drag, which could change the very behaviour being measured, and colonies nesting on the ground are easily disturbed.

Biologging has grown steadily as electronics have shrunk: simple leg rings gave way to satellite tags, then to accelerometers and now cameras. Each step has turned ocean wanderers that were once almost impossible to observe into animals whose daily routines can be mapped.

As sensors get smaller, more species become trackable, and because researchers share their data, many studies can be combined into a single picture of ocean use. That evidence may shape future marine protection around places like the Chagos Archipelago.
